implementation_notes: The direct GoF realization: Component is an abstract base with virtual methods, the base Decorator derives from it, stores the wrapped component (unique_ptr when it owns it, reference/pointer when the wrapped object outlives the wrapper) and forwards every virtual call in its own definitions. Concrete decorators override only the methods they augment and call the base implementation for the rest. It is still the right choice when the chain is assembled at runtime from configuration, plugins or DI - one vtable hop and one allocation per layer - whereas compile-time composition is cheaper but freezes the type (see the mixin variant). The same idea appears in the standard library where a stream delegates to a replaceable std::streambuf (std::ifstream wraps a filebuf), and std::ranges view adaptors are its compile-time relative for sequences.

variants.name: Classic virtual decorator chain
variants.idiom_name: abstract Component + Decorator base holding a pointer/reference to Component; concrete decorators override individual virtual methods
variants.implementation_notes: The direct GoF realization: Component is an abstract base with virtual methods, the base Decorator derives from it, stores the wrapped component (unique_ptr when it owns it, reference/pointer when the wrapped object outlives the wrapper) and forwards every virtual call in its own definitions. Concrete decorators override only the methods they augment and call the base implementation for the rest. It is still the right choice when the chain is assembled at runtime from configuration, plugins or DI - one vtable hop and one allocation per layer - whereas compile-time composition is cheaper but freezes the type (see the mixin variant). The same idea appears in the standard library where a stream delegates to a replaceable std::streambuf (std::ifstream wraps a filebuf), and std::ranges view adaptors are its compile-time relative for sequences.
pitfalls: Slicing: store the wrapped component by pointer or reference - a `Component` data member by value slices the concrete type and silently drops every decorator below it.

Forwarding only the methods you care about: with an abstract base the compiler forces overrides, but if the base is concrete a decorator can inherit behaviour it should have forwarded, so a forgotten forward changes semantics silently.

Ownership style matters: unique_ptr means the wrapper owns the chain and cannot be copied; a raw reference wrapper is fine only while the wrapped object outlives it, and shared_ptr chains can create cycles that keep services alive.

variants.name: Template mixin / CRTP compile-time decorator
variants.idiom_name: template<class Base> struct Wrapper : Base { using Base::Base; ... } - decorator as a mixin class (CRTP for inject-from-above)
variants.implementation_notes: When every layer is known at compile time the wrapper becomes a class template that derives from the wrapped type and adds behaviour, so the whole chain is inlined: no vtable, no per-layer allocation, and the compiler can optimise across the layers (mixin classes are the wrap-from-below form; CRTP injects the behaviour into the host instead). The cost is type identity - `Upper<Counting<FileSource>>` is an unrelated type from `Counting<FileSource>`, so differently decorated stacks cannot share a container without type erasure - which is why the classic virtual variant keeps its place whenever the composition is chosen at runtime. Use it for policy-like, fixed decoration (checksums, bounds checks, logging in hot paths).
pitfalls: Names in a template base are not found unqualified: members of `Base` must be reached as `this->read()` or `Base::read()`, otherwise the code fails to compile or binds an unrelated overload.

Each composition is a distinct type, so a function returning 'a decorated reader' cannot name the growing type - use `auto`, `impl`-style type erasure, or box the chain at the seam where the concrete type must be forgotten.

The mixin inherits from a type it may not own: inheriting from a class without a virtual destructor is fine only if the mixin is never deleted through a `Base*`; deleting polymorphically is undefined behaviour.
